meta.title: Mixolydian, and What the Window's Edges Do
meta.summary: Flattening a degree moves its dot down a fret, which crosses a window's edges in the opposite direction to raising one — and the window clamped at the nut has nothing underneath it for a dot to cross in from.

spans.text: Two things make this window unlike the other four. It's the one clamped at the nut, so it's only four frets wide where the rest are five — part of why its totals sit lower has nothing to do with any mode at all. And because there's nothing below fret 0, no dot can ever cross into this window from underneath — so raising a degree here can lose dots and never gain one, while flattening a degree pulls dots in from above but drops any dot already sitting on fret 0 clean out of the picture.

The three windows this lesson doesn't draw run smaller versions of the same story. The G form and the D form both hold their totals level, seventeen dots either way; the E form loses exactly one, seventeen down to sixteen. None of the three moves by more than a dot, because none of them shares the A form's problem of running out of neck below the nut.

The same single-degree change costs a dot in one window, gains two in another, and barely moves a third — purely because of where each window's edges happen to fall. The dot count is a fact about the frame, not about the mode — never count dots to tell two scales apart.
